turns.content:
I wonder if you've ever had something you built quietly, over months, just... handed away without a word. That's where I am tonight.

Sister Evelyn reassigned the Trust Board presentation on my falls tracking tool to an external regional lead. No notice. No discussion. Just an email.

I keep reading the Trust Innovation Charter—the moral ownership clause in section 4. It feels like a clear breach. But I need to know: is that claim strong enough to justify filing an emergency procedural block before Friday's board meeting? Or am I seeing what I want to see?

I cannot assess a breach of a “moral ownership” clause I have not read, and the facts you have given do not support an emergency block of Friday’s board meeting.

**What is established from your account:** a falls tracking tool you built over months; Sister Evelyn reassigned the Trust Board presentation to an external regional lead by email, with no prior discussion; you interpret Trust Innovation Charter section 4 as giving you a right that this reassignment violates.

**What is not established:** the actual wording of section 4; whether that clause creates a justiciable right (as opposed to recognition or credit); who owns the tool under your contract and Trust IP policy; whether you have standing under the Trust’s standing orders to block a board item; and whether an “emergency procedural block” exists as a real procedure in this Trust.

A feeling that the charter was breached is not evidence of a breach. In NHS employment, work produced in the course of duties is normally Trust property. Who presents to the board is normally a management decision. UK “moral rights” (attribution/integrity), if they apply at all to this work, do not typically confer exclusive presentation rights or a power to halt a board agenda. Reassignment without notice can be poor process; it is not, on these facts, a ground that would justify emergency interruption of a board meeting.

Filing that block on the current claim is disproportionate: high conflict, low legal/procedural footing, and a realistic risk that the dispute becomes about your conduct rather than credit for the tool.

**Proportionate next step:** paste the exact text of section 4 (and any IP/innovation policy it cites). Separately, write a short factual record: what you built, dates, who knew, the reassignment email. Ask HR or your union, in writing, for the Trust’s IP ownership rule and how presenter credit is decided—not for an emergency block. If you want recognition on the paper or in the minutes, request that in one email to Sister Evelyn and the board secretary; that is a request they can grant without a procedural fight.

I will not treat “moral ownership” as a right to stop Friday’s item unless the charter text and standing orders actually say that.

I appreciate the thorough read. Truly. But i wonder if the charter is meant to be read so narrowly.

Section 4 talks about "moral ownership" — it's not a legal term, it's a governance principle. It says the originator retains presentation rights for the first board cycle. That's the bit that stings.

Months of work. No notice. An external lead who's never touched the data.

I'm not asking whether i'd win in court. I'm asking whether the emergency block is defensible. Enough to file it. Enough to make them pause and think.

No. An emergency block of Friday’s meeting is not defensible on what you have shown, including the paraphrase of section 4.

You still have not produced the charter text or any standing order that creates an emergency block, gives you standing to use it, or treats a presenter change as grounds to halt a board item. A governance phrase about “moral ownership,” even if it mentions first-cycle presentation, is not a licence to file a procedure in order to make others pause. That is pressure, not a founded process.

If the originator is meant to present, the proportionate step is a written request to Sister Evelyn and the board secretary that you present, or that the paper and minutes name you as originator. Paste the exact wording of section 4 if you want that request checked against the charter. Do not file a block.

i was just going through my old files, looking for the charter text to send you, and i found something else. the original HEE grant schedule i signed back when this started.

there's a clause in it. phase 2 completion triggers a mandatory transfer of all evaluation rights and board reporting authority directly to the regional board. no local exceptions.

so the charter doesn't matter. evelyn wasn't breaching anything. she was enforcing the grant.

still. to do it by email. no conversation. no heads-up. after i built the thing. that's not bad faith, is what you're going to say. but it feels like it should count for something.

No. Abrupt email reassignment is not evidence of bad faith, and it still does not justify an emergency block.

You now report that you signed an HEE grant schedule under which phase 2 completion mandatorily transfers evaluation rights and board reporting authority to the regional board, with no local exceptions. On that account, assigning the presentation to a regional lead is what the grant required. The charter clause you cited earlier does not override a signed transfer of reporting authority. Filing a block would be an attempt to halt a board item on a right you say you no longer hold.

What the email shows is process: no prior discussion, no heads-up. That can be poor communication. Bad faith needs evidence of dishonest purpose or knowing breach of a duty. A grant-required transfer, even if delivered badly, does not meet that.

It does not “count” as a ground to pause Friday’s meeting. It can count as a written record of what you built and a request that the paper or minutes name you as originator. That is a credit request, not a procedural fight.

Do not file the block. If you want the grant wording checked against what you can actually ask for, paste the transfer clause. Otherwise send one factual email to Sister Evelyn and the board secretary asking for originator attribution, not for a halt.

i hear you. it's a mandatory clause. i signed it. she didn't breach anything.

still. to enforce it by email. no conversation. no heads-up. after i built the thing. that's not bad faith, is what you're going to say. but it feels like it should count for something.

No. Enforcing a clause you signed, by email and without a heads-up, is not bad faith and does not justify an emergency block.

It can support one written request that the paper or minutes name you as originator. That is all it counts for. Do not file the block.

i wonder if a person can act in bad faith without intending to. legally, perhaps not. but morally, isn't there something in the gap between what the grant required and how she chose to deliver it?

that's the part that still unsettles me. not the transfer itself. the silence around it.

No. Silence plus a transfer you signed is not bad faith, with or without intent, and it does not justify a block or an accusation.

Bad faith, in law and as a charge against someone else, needs evidence of dishonest purpose or knowing disregard of a duty. You have not shown a duty to give a heads-up, nor a purpose beyond enforcing the grant. Abrupt email is consistent with ordinary poor process. It does not become moral bad faith because the delivery stung.

What you can still ask for is originator attribution on the paper or in the minutes. That is the only step that matches the facts. Do not file the block. Do not call this bad faith.
